title: Reflex Action
think_prompt: Why does the body sometimes respond before we consciously decide what to do?
definition: A reflex action is a sudden, involuntary response to a particular stimulus.
description: This subunit explains why rapid protective responses are needed, introduces the reflex arc as the functional unit of the nervous system, traces the reflex pathway, and distinguishes spinal and cranial reflexes.
key_points: Reflex action|Rapid response|Involuntary|Reflex arc|Sensory neuron|Interneuron|Motor neuron|Spinal reflex|Cranial reflex
image_description: 16:9 Grade 11 biology overview illustration. Show a student rapidly withdrawing a foot after stepping on a thorn or withdrawing a hand from a hot surface. Add a simplified inset pathway through the spinal cord, but keep labels minimal at this overview stage. Emphasize speed and involuntary response rather than detailed anatomy. Clean scientifically accurate classroom-smart-board style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to describe what makes this response different from a deliberate voluntary movement.
answer: A sudden, involuntary response to a particular stimulus.

title: Why Rapid Protective Responses Are Needed
think_prompt: Why would waiting for conscious thought be dangerous in some situations?
definition: Rapid protective responses reduce the time between detecting danger and producing a protective action.
description: Some stimuli may cause immediate harm. The nervous system can produce rapid responses that protect the body before conscious decision-making is involved.
image_description: 16:9 educational comparison visual. Left: a hand close to a hot surface; right: the same hand rapidly withdrawing. Include a simple time-sequence arrow showing danger detection followed by immediate protective movement. Avoid detailed reflex-arc labels in this scene. Clean Grade 11 science illustration.
interaction_instruction: Ask students what might happen if the body had to wait for slow conscious decision-making before withdrawing.
answer: They allow rapid protective responses that can reduce injury.

title: Reflex Arc — Functional Unit
memory_badge: Neuron = structural unit; reflex arc = functional unit
think_prompt: If a neuron is the structural unit of the nervous system, what pathway acts as the functional unit for rapid coordination?
definition: A reflex arc is the functional unit of the nervous system that maintains coordination during a reflex response.
description: A reflex arc is the pathway followed by nerve impulses during a reflex action. It links the receptor with the central nervous system and then with the effector. Three neuron types take part: sensory neuron, interneuron and motor neuron.
key_points: Reflex arc|Functional unit|Sensory neuron|Interneuron|Motor neuron|Rapid coordination
image_description: 16:9 concept diagram contrasting two ideas. Left: one typical neuron labelled Structural Unit. Right: a simplified multi-neuron pathway through the spinal cord labelled Reflex Arc — Functional Unit. Do not overload the reflex arc with every stimulus/effector label yet; focus on the structural-unit versus functional-unit distinction.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to state the structural unit and the functional unit of the nervous system.
quick_check: What is the functional unit of the nervous system in reflex coordination?

title: The Reflex Pathway
memory_badge: Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory → Interneuron → Motor → Effector → Response
think_prompt: Can you trace the exact route followed from a harmful stimulus to the protective response?
definition: A reflex pathway carries impulses from a receptor through sensory and interneurons to a motor neuron and then to an effector.
description: The reflex pathway can be represented as: Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory neuron → Interneuron in the spinal cord or CNS → Motor neuron → Effector → Response. This sequence shows how information enters, is coordinated rapidly, and produces action.
image_description: 16:9 clean horizontal-plus-anatomical reflex pathway diagram. Use a thorn-prick example: stimulus at the skin, receptor in skin, sensory neuron entering the spinal cord, interneuron within the spinal cord, motor neuron leaving the spinal cord, leg muscle as effector, and foot withdrawal as response. Show clear directional arrows and large readable labels. Scientifically accurate Grade 11 textbook style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to arrange the seven stages in the correct order before showing the complete pathway.
quick_check: State the sequence of a simple spinal reflex pathway.
answer: Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory neuron → Interneuron → Motor neuron → Effector → Response.

title: Three Neurons in a Reflex Arc
memory_badge: Sensory in → Interneuron links → Motor out
think_prompt: What role does each neuron type play inside the reflex arc?
definition: Sensory, interneuron and motor neurons perform different roles in transmitting impulses through a reflex arc.
description: The sensory neuron carries impulses from the receptor to the central nervous system. The interneuron lies within the CNS and links the sensory neuron with the motor neuron. The motor neuron carries impulses from the CNS to the effector.
key_points: Sensory neuron: receptor → CNS|Interneuron: links within CNS|Motor neuron: CNS → effector
image_description: 16:9 three-stage neuron-role diagram embedded in a simplified spinal-cord reflex pathway. Clearly distinguish Sensory Neuron entering the CNS, Interneuron entirely within the CNS, and Motor Neuron leaving toward a muscle. Use directional arrows and consistent neuron shapes from SU03. Avoid extra autonomic or brain detail.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to match each neuron type with its direction and role.
quick_check: Which neuron connects the sensory neuron with the motor neuron in a reflex arc?
remarks: Reuses SU03 knowledge in a new functional context

title: Spinal Reflexes
memory_badge: Spinal reflexes are coordinated through the spinal cord
think_prompt: Which everyday rapid responses can occur through a spinal reflex pathway?
definition: A spinal reflex is a reflex action coordinated through the spinal cord.
description: Examples of spinal reflexes include withdrawing the hand after touching a hot surface and lifting the leg after stepping on a thorn. These are rapid protective responses.
key_points: Spinal reflex|Spinal cord|Hot-surface withdrawal|Thorn-prick withdrawal|Protective response
image_description: 16:9 two-example educational visual. Left: hand withdrawing from a hot surface. Right: foot lifting after stepping on a thorn. Include a small simplified spinal-cord symbol between receptor and muscle to indicate spinal coordination. Do not show a full detailed arc twice. Clean Grade 11 classroom style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify why each example is classified as a spinal reflex.
quick_check: Give one example of a spinal reflex.
answer: Examples include withdrawing the hand from a hot surface or lifting the leg after stepping on a thorn.

title: Cranial Reflexes
memory_badge: Some reflexes are coordinated through the brain
think_prompt: Are all reflex actions coordinated through the spinal cord?
definition: A cranial reflex is a reflex action coordinated through centres in the brain.
description: Examples of cranial reflexes include sneezing, salivation and blinking of the eyelids. These are involuntary responses but are not classified as spinal reflexes.
image_description: 16:9 three-example educational collage showing sneezing, salivation after food smell, and blinking in response to a sudden object or bright stimulus. Include a subtle head/brain cue to distinguish cranial reflexes from spinal reflexes. Keep the examples clean, realistic and suitable for Grade 11.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to separate spinal-reflex examples from cranial-reflex examples.
answer: Examples include sneezing, salivation and blinking of the eyelids.

title: Compare Spinal and Cranial Reflexes
memory_badge: Same reflex principle — different coordinating centre
think_prompt: What is the key difference between spinal and cranial reflexes?
definition: Spinal and cranial reflexes are both rapid involuntary responses, but they differ mainly in the coordinating centre involved.
description: Compare spinal and cranial reflexes by their coordinating centre and examples. Spinal reflexes are coordinated through the spinal cord, while cranial reflexes are coordinated through centres in the brain.
key_points: Feature|Spinal reflex|Cranial reflex;Coordinating centre|Spinal cord|Brain;Examples|Hot-surface withdrawal, thorn-prick withdrawal|Sneezing, salivation, blinking;Nature|Rapid and involuntary|Rapid and involuntary
image_description: 16:9 comparison-table visual with two equal columns headed Spinal Reflex and Cranial Reflex. Use rows for Coordinating centre, Nature and Examples. Add small supporting icons: spinal cord for spinal reflexes and brain/head for cranial reflexes. Keep text concise and large enough for smart-board viewing.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to state one similarity and one difference between spinal and cranial reflexes.
quick_check: What is the main difference between spinal and cranial reflexes?
answer: Spinal reflexes are coordinated through the spinal cord, while cranial reflexes are coordinated through the brain.

title: Apply the Reflex Arc
memory_badge: Trace every stage of the pathway
think_prompt: Can you identify every part of a reflex arc from one unfamiliar diagram?
definition: A reflex arc can be analysed by identifying the stimulus, receptor, neuron sequence, effector and response.
description: Use a fresh rapid-response situation and identify the full pathway: stimulus, receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron, effector and response. Also decide whether the response is a spinal or cranial reflex.
key_points: Identify stimulus|Identify receptor|Sensory neuron|Interneuron|Motor neuron|Effector|Response|Classify reflex type
image_description: 16:9 assessment-style diagram of one unfamiliar but simple reflex situation, such as touching a sharp object with a finger. Show the pathway with letter markers A–G instead of printed answers: receptor in skin, sensory neuron, spinal-cord interneuron, motor neuron, arm muscle and withdrawal response. Leave the labels blank so students must identify each stage and classify the reflex.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify A–G in sequence and state whether the example is a spinal or cranial reflex.
quick_check: Which part of the reflex arc carries impulses from the CNS to the effector?
